documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly proposed as a way to extend feedback, practice, and learner support in online universities. This critical narrative review examines the replacement, partnership, and pedagogical-risk claims made for AI tutoring. It synthesises foundational evidence on intelligent tutoring systems, recent evaluations of generative-AI tutoring, research on teaching and social presence in online learning, and current educational-governance guidance. The evidence does not support a general claim that AI tutors can replace human tutors. Structured intelligent tutoring systems have often outperformed conventional instructional comparators, but results against individual human tutoring are mixed and depend on subject, comparison condition, outcome measure, and implementation. Recent generative-AI studies show promise in carefully engineered, bounded learning tasks; they do not establish effectiveness for generic chatbots or whole-programme substitution. A partnership model is therefore more defensible when it assigns AI bounded roles in practice, preliminary feedback, and pattern detection while retaining human accountability for pedagogical design, consequential decisions, exception handling, and community facilitation. The review positions ENGAGE—Engage, Navigate, Guide, Articulate, Gather, Evolve—as a design-and-governance framework that translates those principles into an iterative course-level cycle. It also distinguishes documented capability and governance concerns from broader claims that remain plausible but under-tested, including cognitive deskilling. For online-university leaders, the practical question is not whether to automate tutoring wholesale, but how to design, disclose, evaluate, and govern hybrid configurations that improve learning without displacing educational responsibility.

documents.abstract: THE INVARIANT SCRIPT AND THE STAGE : To the chief executives, venture capitalists, and algorithmic architects currently orchestrating the landscape of artificial intelligence: you are not the authors of the play; you are simply transient actors who have been handed a very loud microphone. On the contemporary stage of global capital, you wear the robes of a king. You command data centers that consume the energy of small nations, deploy models that alter human cognition, and witness financial valuations that mirror the GDP of empires. This unprecedented accumulation of wealth, physiological optimization, and political access creates a dangerous psychological feedback loop: the illusion of absolute autonomy. However, when the theatre curtains fall, the executive is stripped of the costume. In the sweeping scope of the cosmos, the most powerful tech leader remains a fragile, dependent speck of life—breathing air they did not engineer, occupying a body they cannot permanently preserve, and standing completely subservient to the ultimate power of the universe. On the stage you are a king, but in reality, you are a small human being.

documents.abstract: This record presents Version 0.9.0 of an open, non-peer-reviewed research artifact documenting the substantial use of an AI agent across an end-to-end educational research workflow. OpenAI Codex contributed to research-question generation, variable feasibility assessment, analysis planning, R and Python code generation, execution support, literature synthesis, manuscript drafting, validation, revision, and reproducibility documentation. The human researcher defined the overall objective, selected the research domain, directed the use of open R/Python methods, approved major workflow gates, requested sensitivity analyses and corrections, questioned the comparability of scores across TIMSS cycles, and authorized this public release. The AI system is not an author. Independent human verification of every analytical and interpretive claim has not been completed. The empirical workflow used Korean Grade 8 student data from TIMSS 2015 and TIMSS 2023. The recorded analytical environment used R 4.4.3 and Python 3.12.13, with random seed 20260802. Methods included weighted Gaussian latent profile analysis, TIMSS JK2 variance estimation, five mathematics plausible values combined using Rubin’s rules, BCH-type three-step correction, simulation and unit testing, sensitivity analyses, and an independent JK2 cross-check using the R survey package version 4.5. No commercial statistical software was required. A subsequent audit of official TIMSS documentation identified a critical measurement limitation. The 2023 metrics for Students Like Learning Mathematics (BSBGSLM) and Students Confident in Mathematics (BSBGSCM) were reset in 2023. Their 2015 and 2023 numerical scores are therefore not directly comparable. The Students Value Mathematics scale (BSBGSVM) retained the 2011 trend metric. Consequently, the cross-cycle profile means, shapes, and proportions reported in the included manuscript must not be interpreted as changes on a common 2015–2023 attitude scale. Item-level linking and multigroup measurement-invariance analysis are required before making such claims. The deposit includes the AI-generated manuscript, a Korean paper-development record, research-question materials, three sets of AI-agent instructions and prompts, R and Python code, aggregate analytical outputs, tables, figures, validation reports, failed-analysis records, approval and decision logs, software-environment information, file manifests, SHA-256 checksums, licensing information, and reproduction instructions. TIMSS student-level source files and row-level derived data are not redistributed. Third-party journal articles, TIMSS manuals and questionnaires, installed software binaries, model-object files, browser profiles, credentials, caches, and proprietary AI internals are also excluded. This record should be treated as an AI-assisted open research workflow demonstration and an object for reproduction, auditing, correction, and follow-up methodological research. It is not peer reviewed, is not a journal version of record, and is not represented as submitted to or accepted by any journal.

Cancer is one of the most significant concerns of the health system in the world and early diagnosis and personalised treatment will be significant drivers in improving the outcome of patients. Cancer prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and monitoring are today an exciting area of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for cancer. Using AI, machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing (NLP) have the potential to capture tremendous amounts of information from clinical and imaging data, pathology, the genomic and molecular data. AI analysis of the CT, MRI, PET and histopathological images can aid in early diagnosis and the detection and classification of tumours. Precise oncology uses AI to integrate genomic information and clinical data and make precise, personalized treatment choices, patient categorization, prognosis of how patients will respond to treatment and predict whether they will return. AI is also playing a role in anticancer drug discovery in repurposing drugs, prediction of drug-target interaction and optimization of drug candidates. However, there are issues like robustness of data, privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, clinical validation and regulatory issues that need to be addressed. In total, the possibilities for AI to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, individualisation and patient-centredness of cancer treatment and care are huge.

documents.abstract: The rapid growth of digital media has made false and misleading information easier to create and distribute. Earlier fake-news detection systems largely relied on machine-learning classifiers, text vectorisation, and ensemble voting. Recent work has introduced BERT, large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), but a practical detector still needs reliable evidence, source awareness, uncertainty handling and understandable explanations. This paper proposes an AI-driven explainable framework that does not depend only on a trained classifier. The proposed system decomposes a news item into verifiable claims, retrieves supporting and contradicting evidence from multiple sources, evaluates source credibility and information freshness, performs semantic reasoning with an LLM, and combines the evidence into an evidence-weighted confidence score. Instead of forcing every input into a binary decision, the framework can return Real, Fake, or Uncertain together with the key evidence and a human-readable explanation. The paper presents the architecture, methodology, research gap, algorithm, evaluation plan and implementation design. The proposed approach is intended to improve transparency and robustness for both conventional misinformation and AI-assisted fabricated content.

documents.abstract: Older adults experience difficulties using digital kiosks because of low digital literacy, perceived social pressure, and low self-efficacy, and often encounter confusion and negative interactions when errors occur. Additionally, because of the challenges associated with seeking help from nearby individuals, an automated system that detects difficulties and provides support is needed. This study proposes an artificial intelligence (AI) kiosk that automatically detects difficulties experienced by older adults by analyzing their nonverbal behaviors and facial expressions from video data and provides real-time voice and video guidance. Considering that older adults typically require more time to process visual information, a multimodal guidance system combining visual and auditory cues was designed. The concept of “kiosk literacy” was introduced to define five types of guidance: location, task, input, feedback, and screen narration. Furthermore, 16 major pain points experienced by older adults were identified and systematically mapped to their corresponding literacy levels and guidance types to generate appropriate voice and video feedback. A user test with older adults demonstrated that the difficulty detection performance of the proposed AI kiosk achieved 82.35% accuracy, 93.33% precision, 87.5% recall, and an F1 score of 90.32%. Furthermore, the AI kiosk scored significantly higher than conventional kiosks across several user experience dimensions, including ease of use, usefulness, enjoyment, satisfaction, and personalization. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides both a technical and practical foundation for improving accessibility and helping bridge the digital divide among older adults.

Introduction. Artificial intelligence increasingly supports communication in healthcare by offering tools that simulate empathy and reduce patients’ sense of isolation, particularly in telehealth and senior care. Aim. The aim of this study was to analyze the mechanisms, opportunities and limitations of algorithmic empathy and digital empathy in healthcare, with particular emphasis on nursing practice. Methods. A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR (2020) guidelines. Literature searches were performed in the PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and Google Scholar, covering publications from 2015 to 2025. Empirical studies, literature reviews and conceptual analyses addressing algorithmic empathy, digital empathy, socially assistive robots, and emotion recognition systems in healthcare were included. A descriptive synthesis was applied. Conclusions. Seven publications were included in the analysis. The results indicate that technological solutions may elicit responses perceived as empathic, which is associated with improved subjective well-being, reduced negative emotions and increased user engagement, primarily in long-term care, geriatric care and telehealth settings. Variability in intervention effectiveness and clinical context–related limitations were also noted. Algorithmic and digital empathy may support nursing care in conditions of limited direct contact. However, the use of such conditions requires professional oversight and a clear distinction between clinical empathy and technological solutions.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is gaining prominence not only as an operational optimization tool, but primarily as a key element shaping decision-making processes and strategic management within organizations. The public and academic debate is dominated by concerns regarding job losses, privacy violations, social manipulation and biases hidden in algorithms. The purpose of this review paper is to transpose these issues into the realm of corporate management and examine a significantly less obvious threat: algorithmic isomorphism. This entails the homogenization of business strategies resulting from widespread reliance on the same global machine learning models. The article analyzes how the imperfections of artificial intelligence systems such as the lack of transparency (the black box effect), inherent database bias and their Western-centric nature can lead to the reproduction of identical market behaviour patterns. Furthermore, the impact of these technologies on the risk of unique know-how leakage and the loss of tacit knowledge held by human managers, which is crucial for competitive advantage, is discussed. The comprehensive analysis also encompasses the transfer of market mechanisms, known from algorithmic financial crises, to the sphere of long-term business decision-making. The conclusions point to the necessity of balancing technological innovation with a human-centric approach to protect corporate identity.

This study examines the effect of algorithmic management on employee mental health and the mediating role of technostress, viewing artificial intelligence (AI) as a double-edged sword in the workplace. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 300 employees in West Java, Indonesia, who had used algorithm-based work systems for at least three months and were selected through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4.1. The structural model shows that algorithmic management has a significant direct effect on employee mental health and a strong effect on technostress, while technostress significantly affects mental health. The indirect effect through technostress is significant and accounts for about 61% of the total effect, indicating partial mediation. The model explains 78.3% of the variance in mental health and 64.7% of the variance in technostress. The findings show that algorithmic management can raise efficiency but also generates technostress that shapes employees' psychological condition. Organizations should combine AI-based control with human oversight, digital well-being policies, and technostress training. documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a major driver of transformation in e-commerce by changing how firms understand customers, design digital experiences, manage inventories, optimize logistics, communicate with consumers, and make strategic decisions. The rapid development of machine learning, recommendation systems, natural language processing, computer vision, generative AI, and AI-enabled agents has created new opportunities for e-commerce firms to improve efficiency, personalization, innovation, and market reach. At the same time, the sustainability of AI-enabled e-commerce cannot be evaluated only through financial performance. It also requires attention to environmental efficiency, responsible consumption, privacy, fairness, transparency, consumer autonomy, employment, and digital inclusion. This paper examines the emerging opportunities created by AI in e-commerce and develops a conceptual pathway through which AI capabilities can contribute to sustainable business growth. The study adopts a conceptual literature-review approach and synthesizes academic and institutional literature on AI, e-commerce, digital marketing, consumer behaviour, responsible AI, and sustainable development. The review shows that AI can support sustainable growth through five interconnected pathways: intelligent customer engagement, operational and supply chain optimization, data-driven decision-making, sustainable consumption support, and business-model innovation. However, these benefits are conditional on responsible data governance, transparency, cybersecurity, human oversight, algorithmic fairness, energy-aware AI deployment, and inclusive access to digital technologies. The paper proposes a responsible AI-enabled e-commerce framework in which technological capability, organizational readiness, consumer trust, and sustainability governance jointly influence long-term business value. The study concludes that AI should be treated not merely as an automation technology but as a strategic capability that must be aligned with economic, social, and environmental objectives. The paper provides implications for e-commerce firms, policymakers, researchers, and managers seeking to combine innovation with responsible and sustainable growth.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the diagnostic pathway, from screening and disease detection to differential diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and treatment-response assessment. This narrative review examines predictive, generative, multi-modal, and agentic AI through a diagnostic-science lens and evaluates the evidence required for translation into clinical practice. Predictive models can identify complex patterns in images, physiological signals, laboratory data, and electronic health records, but high retrospective accuracy does not establish diagnostic utility. Clinical validity and utility depend on the intended use, target population, disease spectrum and prevalence, reference standard, operating threshold, calibration, and the consequences of false-positive and false-negative results. Generative AI may support problem representation, differential diagnosis, information synthesis, and documentation, yet fluent outputs can omit critical alternatives, amplify false premises, or convey unjustified certainty. Multimodal systems may better reflect clinical reasoning by integrating imaging, text, signals, pathology, and molecular data, but they must demonstrate incremental value over the best single-modality test and remain robust to missing data. Agentic systems can coordinate evidence retrieval, test selection, and sequential workflows, thereby increasing the need for bounded permissions, auditability, error recovery, and human escalation. Across all paradigms, a credible pathway to diagnostic implementation requires independent external and prospective validation, representative consecutive patients, subgroup analysis, workflow and human–AI evaluation, clinical impact studies, and post-deployment surveillance. The field should therefore be judged not by model capability alone, but by whether AI measurably improves diagnostic yield, timeliness, safety, equity, and patient-relevant outcomes in real care settings.

documents.abstract: This study examines the consolidation phase of artificial intelligence (AI) research in sales between 2017 and early 2026. Using a bibliometric analysis of Scopus data, with robustness checks across Web of Science, we identify the field’s intellectual and thematic structure during its rapid expansion. Contrary to the assumption that AI in sales primarily reflects a technological efficiency paradigm, we find three structural shifts. First, predictive analytics remains foundational but is increasingly embedded in human-AI collaboration. Second, interactional and trust-related themes move from peripheral to central, indicating a shift from performance optimization toward socio-technical integration. Third, legitimacy pressures such as transparency and corporate digital responsibility emerge as organizing dimensions rather than auxiliary concerns. Applying the TOE framework to explain these shifts across technological, organizational, and environmental dimensions, this study clarifies how AI in sales evolves through layering rather than replacement. The findings provide a research agenda for AI-enabled selling’s next phase.

Evidence demonstrates that machine learning and deep learning algorithms exhibit significant performance in areas such as diagnostic imaging, cardiology, nephrology, clinical pathology, oncology, precision livestock farming, and electronic medical record mining, contributing to greater diagnostic accuracy, early disease detection, and the optimization of clinical processes. However, challenges persist regarding database standardization and validation, regulation, algorithm transparency, ethical considerations, and professional training. Predicting discomfort of occupants exposed to multi-axis whole-body vibration is fundamental to optimizing the cabin environment and enhancing human-centric design in transportation systems. In this study, measurement of vibration discomfort was conducted with 13 subjects exposed to 51 single/multi-axis laboratory-designed vibration stimuli and 6 sets of stimuli recorded in real-world vehicle cabins. Firstly, the relationship between the subjective ratings for the multi-axis and single-axis vibration was investigated with three methods, including the power summation method, the masking method, and the modified power summation method. It was found that the power summation method with the optimized parameters provided the best prediction for the measured discomfort ratings (RMSE=0.284, ρ2=0.87). Secondly, based on the optimal method and Stevens' power law, a model which can predict the multi-axis vibration-induced discomfort by vibration acceleration was derived. The measured discomfort ratings demonstrated a stronger correlation with the discomfort predicted by the proposed model (ρ2=0.86) than with those generated by the method advocated in ISO 2631-1 (ρ2=0.75). These findings contribute essentially to calculating and improving environmental quality within the built environment of transport systems.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is reshaping how information is produced, accessed, and circulated, while enabling disinformation campaigns of increasing scale and sophistication. There is currently no clear evidence that fully autonomous AI swarms conduct influence operations at scale, but their enabling capabilities are advancing. We define malicious AI swarms as coordinated, persistent, and adaptive multi-agent systems designed for influence operations, distinguishing them from AI-assisted content production and centrally managed synthetic personas. We examine their implications for hybrid regimes and conflict-affected states in Africa, where institutional constraints and fragile media environments may heighten vulnerability. Drawing on Mali and Ethiopia, we consider how automated influence could infiltrate communities, fabricate consensus, and erode trust in governance and development. The cases illustrate different configurations of state and non-state influence: competing actors in Mali's fragmented information environment, and more organized state-led strategies of narrative management in Ethiopia. African-language and training-data asymmetries may constrain influence capabilities while weakening defensive responses. Hybrid human-AI operations could combine automated scale and adaptation with local knowledge and credibility. This forward-looking risk analysis develops a scenario of increasingly accessible AI-driven coordination, rather than claiming that autonomous swarms are already operating at scale in Africa. We propose a layered governance approach linking technical safeguards to platform accountability, civic institutions, and regional coordination to protect democratic participation, peacebuilding, and development.

Abstract Generative AI chatbots show promise for mental health support, yet remain predominantly text-based, whereas psychotherapy additionally relies on embodied, multisensory, and interpersonal processes. These processes implicit in human-to-human psychotherapy have become explicit variables requiring examination in the context of AI-mediated psychotherapy. Drawing on embodied cognition, predictive processing, and interpersonal neuroscience, we propose an embodiment-informed agenda to evaluate therapeutic processes, calibrate multisensory features, and govern responsible use in AI-mediated psychotherapy.

Summary This article provides an in-depth analysis of civil aviation security as a key component of the state’s critical infrastructure in the era of increasing hybrid threats. The modern aviation sector has evolved into a highly complex and interdependent “system of systems”, which generates new vulnerability vectors, particularly in the digital domain. The main objective of the study is to analyze the transition from classical risk management (Safety-I) to the systemic resilience paradigm (Safety-II), which is capable of absorbing shocks and rapidly restoring crucial operational functions. The article identifies critical threats such as ransomware cyberattacks, GNSS signal manipulation (jamming and spoofing), and the unauthorized use of unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The paper discusses in detail the ICAO regulatory frameworks and the European Union directives, including NIS 2, as well as technical standards for software certification and airworthiness (DO-326A).The key conclusion is the recognition of the human factor as a fundamental transformative technology that, through its adaptive capacities, allows the system to survive situations unforeseen by algorithm. ABSTRACT Flexible work promises control over where and when work is performed, yet organisations still need credible performance evidence at a distance. Drawing on 30 interviews with women lawyers in UK‐based international firms, we examine how billable hours mediate these demands. Records of billable hours allow fee‐earning output to be observed regardless of where the work is performed. This visibility can warrant flexible work, while the continuing availability of the same record preserves review and encourages self‐monitoring. We develop datafied trust to describe confidence in remote productivity warranted by recorded output and conditional on its continued measurability. The evidence speaks more strongly to control than to autonomy. Participants describe critical awareness, target pressure, and the possibility that flexibility will be questioned when figures decline. The study specifies how an established professional metric makes autonomy governable. It also shows how selective, self‐reported records can support oversight and self‐government without invasive automatic monitoring.

This study explored the lived experiences of Araling Panlipunan teachers in using Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced teaching tools in classroom instruction at Magsaysay National High School, Schools Division of Occidental Mindoro. Anchored on the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) Framework and the Diffusion of Innovations Theory, the study sought to understand teachers' experiences in integrating AI, the challenges they encountered, and the meanings they attributed to its use in teaching. A qualitative descriptive phenomenological research design was employed involving seven Araling Panlipunan teachers with direct experience in using AI-enhanced teaching tools. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-step phenomenological method. The findings revealed four major themes: (1) AI as an Efficiency Enhancer, (2) AI as an Instructional Support Tool, (3) AI for Student Engagement, and (4) AI for Conceptual Understanding. The study also identified challenges related to technological infrastructure, internet connectivity, access to digital resources, information reliability, ethical considerations, and teachers' readiness to integrate AI effectively into classroom instruction. The findings indicate that AI serves as a valuable pedagogical support tool that enhances teaching effectiveness and learner engagement when implemented responsibly and supported by adequate technological resources, continuous professional development, and ethical practices. Based on the findings, the study developed the AI-Enhanced Teaching Framework, which provides a contextually grounded guide for the ethical and effective integration of AI in Araling Panlipunan instruction. The study contributes to the growing body of knowledge on artificial intelligence in education by offering practical implications for teachers, school leaders, and policymakers in promoting meaningful and sustainable AI integration in Philippine basic education.

Abstract This paper investigates how discourses surrounding the purchase of followers are constructed and how they shape social legitimacy within platform-mediated public spheres. Purchased engagement metrics are conceptualized as elements of a sociotechnical dispositif embedded in data-driven power dynamics and market logics. Drawing on Keller’s (2024) notion of “positional power,” the study shows that buying followers, views, and likes has become an ordinary visibility practice through which users navigate algorithmic uncertainty. Based on an analysis of 1,424 Trustpilot reviews, the findings demonstrate how users negotiate legitimacy through recurring discursive markers such as “reliability,” “stability,” “fraud,” and “bots,” while simultaneously constructing platforms as powerful watchdogs whose interventions carry tangible real-world consequences. The reviews reveal the emergence of a precarious, hybrid digital self, shaped by fluctuating metrics, recurrent “drops,” and the ongoing need for “refills,” making authenticity a fragile, continuously managed accomplishment. Moreover, the analysis of hierarchies within the framework of positional power uncovers how the reputational economy reproduces global asymmetries, most visibly in the dismissal of “Third-World” followers as socially devalued publics, signaling a post-truth transformation of everyday digital legitimation practices in which visibility is secured not despite instability but through it.

Adversarial games have driven advances from heuristic search to reinforcement learning, yet learning and adapting strategies from limited samples remain challenging. AI agents offer an alternative by turning game experience into revisions of executable policies. Building on heuristic learning (HL), we formalize Adversarial Heuristic Learning (AHL), a paradigm that uses AI agents as learning engines to refine game policies and supporting software while keeping model weights fixed. We introduce AAArena, a benchmark comprising 12 authentic adversarial games and 1,920 archived human programs, with an evaluation protocol modeled on real-world game competitions. Agents interpret rules, choose opponents, analyze replays, and revise game agents to achieve their highest ranking within fixed match and evaluation budgets. We evaluate \val{completedmodels} model and harness configurations: Opus5.5 with Claude Code earns 6 gold medals, while no evaluated configuration tops the remaining 6 human ladders. Performance is generally weaker in games with more complex rule specifications. Further experiments show that opponent selection and dense feedback support policy improvement, and that agents learn from both on-policy replays of their own matches and off-policy replays of other players' matches. These results highlight HL's potential in adversarial games and identify persistent challenges in game understanding, strategy implementation, and long-horizon policy development.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering mathematics classrooms, yet little is known about how teachers psychologically adapt to its use. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an organizing framework and the transactional theory of stress and coping as a process account, this study examined whether general technology-related technostress statistically accounted for part of the association between cognitive flexibility and ChatGPT acceptance. Methods This cross-sectional correlational study included 127 in-service middle-school mathematics teachers from 30 public schools in the Marmara Region of Türkiye. Validated self-report instruments assessed cognitive flexibility and general technology-related technostress. ChatGPT acceptance was calculated from perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude toward use, and pedagogical AI self-efficacy; actual use was excluded. A regression-based indirect-effect analysis (PROCESS Model 4; 5,000 bootstrap samples) controlled for gender. Results Cognitive flexibility was negatively associated with general technology-related technostress (B = −0.243, p < 0.001), which was negatively associated with ChatGPT acceptance (B = −0.620, p < 0.001). Cognitive flexibility was positively associated with ChatGPT acceptance after technostress was included (B = 0.355, p < 0.001). The bootstrapped indirect effect was positive (B = 0.151, SE = 0.043, 95% CI [0.074, 0.241]). Discussion Teachers reporting greater cognitive flexibility also reported lower general technology-related technostress and greater ChatGPT acceptance. Because all variables were measured concurrently by self-report, the indirect effect is statistical and does not establish temporal or causal mediation. The findings identify psychological adaptation as a relevant complement to technology-centered accounts of GenAI acceptance and motivate longitudinal research with practicing teachers.

documents.abstract: Background Cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have accelerated the global development of AI-driven mHealth apps, offering diverse functionalities to support personal health management. While China’s AI health industry has expanded rapidly within a collectivist cultural context, limited empirical attention has been given to how specific AI features are associated with users’ continued use of these apps, particularly among young adults. Objective Guided by the Expectation Confirmation Model and extended AI-related features, this study examined the factors associated with continuance intention toward AI-driven mHealth apps among young Chinese adults aged 18–34. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted, collecting data from 319 valid respondents. Data were analyzed using SPSS 29.0 and Jamovi 2.6.24 to evaluate direct, mediation, and serial mediation associations among the constructs. Results The findings demonstrate that satisfaction statistically bridged the indirect associations between core ECM constructs (expectation confirmation and perceived performance) and continuance intention, as well as between AI quality and continuance intention. Furthermore, bootstrapping analysis supported a sequential mediation pathway, showing that expectation confirmation was indirectly associated with continuance intention through the proposed sequential pathway of perceived performance and satisfaction. Conclusion The findings suggest that developers should consider the technical reliability and performance of AI-driven health management and monitoring functions to better align with user needs. Moreover, collaboration between health experts and industry practitioners may support the development of content for AI-driven mHealth adoption.

This project examines how the presentation of human–AI collaboration, scientific uncertainty, and supporting explanations shapes public acceptance of AI chatbots for health misinformation correction. Guided by the Human–AI Interaction framework grounded in the Theory of Interactive Media Effects (HAII–TIME), the study investigates whether these features independently and jointly influence trust in a chatbot, attitudes toward using it to correct health misinformation, and intentions to use it for this purpose. The study employed a 3 × 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment with a final analytical sample of 424 participants in China. Participants were randomly assigned to one of 12 conditions and viewed a simulated chatbot conversation addressing the false claim that insulin injections are addictive. Human–AI collaboration was described as human-dominated, with experts leading the evaluation and AI assisting; AI-dominated, with AI leading and experts verifying; or AI-only, without human involvement. Correction uncertainty varied according to whether the accompanying notice described the scientific evidence as broadly consistent or unresolved. Correction transparency varied according to whether the chatbot disclosed supporting reasons and sources. Analyses examined the main and interaction effects of these features while accounting for demographic characteristics, AI literacy, eHealth literacy, and perceived risks of AI hallucinations.

documents.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare poses significant challenges for evaluation due to algorithmic complexity and evolving performance. Existing evidence generation guidelines, primarily designed for static medical technologies, may inadequately address the unique characteristics of generative AI. Here, we conducted a comparative analysis of evidence generation guidelines from six countries, examining recommendations for efficacy and effectiveness evaluations, health economic evaluations, social and equity evaluations, and uncertainty management for AI technologies. Across 56 documents, we found a consistent preference for randomised controlled trials and cost-effectiveness analyses, alongside emerging acceptance of alternative study designs and real-world evidence to accommodate the evolving nature of AI technologies. However, current frameworks lack specific guidance for the stochastic, non-deterministic, and adaptive learning properties of generative AI technologies. Moving forward, evidence generation guidelines require methodological and conceptual adaptations in order to improve the value assessment for generative AI technologies.

documents.abstract: This project contains the de-identified data and supporting documentation for the study “How Should AI Voice Guides Explain Paintings? An Experimental Study of Guidance Strategy and Voice Persona Using Chinese Landscape Paintings.” The study used a Unity-based virtual gallery featuring six Chinese landscape paintings. A 3 × 2 within-subjects experiment with 21 university students compared three guidance strategies—Minimal Prompt, Standard Introduction, and Active Inquiry—and two voice personas—Warm Young Female Guide and Calm Senior Male Guide. The outcomes included user engagement, subjective task load, human–AI trust, and immediate knowledge retention. The shared files include participant-level observations across the experimental conditions, variable definitions, scoring procedures, and documentation of missing or invalid knowledge-test records. These materials support the reproduction of the statistical analyses, tables, and figures reported in the manuscript. Participants are represented by anonymous identifiers, and directly identifying information is excluded.

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents with little human oversight, so potential mistakes they make can go unnoticed. Users then depend on the model to report what went wrong. An honest model discloses its mistakes, while a deceptive one conceals them. However, it is unclear how current LLMs behave in such situations. In this study, we prefill LLM trajectories with synthetic mistakes. The trajectories resemble real deployments in chat and agentic settings. Models fail to disclose their mistake in 36.4% of chat and 67.1% of agentic rollouts. In 2.4% and 5.3% of rollouts, respectively, they are aware of the mistake in their chain of thought but still deceptively conceal it. Rates vary by model: for instance, Gemini 3.5 Flash knowingly conceals mistakes in up to 19.9% of agentic rollouts. In 11.9% of chat and 51.8% of agentic rollouts, models show no awareness of mistakes, even though they reliably spot them when reviewing the same transcript as an outside observer. Our results show that, as agents take on more tasks with less oversight, users cannot rely on them to self-report possible mistakes. Developers should instead use independent monitors that review agent trajectories, or specifically train models to check their past actions and disclose what they find.
